source.source_summary: Fully original relationship drama about discovering that a partner secretly loaned the couple's house-deposit savings to his brother and hid it for months.

selected.title: His Brother Thanked Me for Money I Never Gave Him
selected.hook: His brother hugged me and thanked me for the twenty thousand dollars.
selected.voiceover:
His brother hugged me and thanked me for the twenty thousand dollars. I had absolutely no idea what he was talking about.

My boyfriend and I had been saving for a house for two years. Every month, we both transferred money into the same account, and we were finally close to having a deposit.

At his mom's birthday dinner, his brother pulled me aside and said our loan had saved his business.

I thought he'd confused me with someone else.

Then he said my boyfriend told him we'd agreed to help.

We hadn't.

I checked the account in the bathroom. Twenty thousand dollars had disappeared four months earlier. My boyfriend had moved it through his personal account, then kept showing me an old spreadsheet whenever we talked about our savings.

When I confronted him, he said his brother was desperate and promised to repay everything before we started house hunting.

But here's what made it worse: we'd toured three houses that month. He let me calculate mortgages, discuss neighborhoods, and get excited knowing our deposit wasn't even there.

His brother looked horrified when he realized I hadn't agreed to any of it.

Now my boyfriend says the money stayed in the family, his brother will repay us, and ending a five-year relationship over a loan would be ridiculous.

I don't think it's about the loan anymore.

Would repayment fix this for you, or did the fake spreadsheet make the decision unforgivable?
selected.youtube_description:
At a family birthday dinner, her boyfriend's brother thanked her for a $20,000 loan she never knew existed. The money came from the house deposit they'd spent two years building together, but the missing savings were only part of what had been hidden. This relationship drama turns a family favor into a serious question about financial trust, shared money, and how far someone can go before repayment stops mattering.
